previous_implementation_evidence.heading: RIP_GOTOXY
previous_implementation_evidence.text: This command sets the position of the text cursor in the TTY Text window, if it is active. If inactive (if the dimensions are 0,0,0,0), then this command is ignored. This command is equivalent to the ANSI/VT-100 command goto x/y, `<Esc>[x;yH`, except that the coordinates of that ANSI command are 1-based and the coordinates of this RIPscrip command are 0-based.

previous_implementation_evidence.heading: Flags
previous_implementation_evidence.text: It should be noted that there are some fundamental differences in nature from the extended text window command and the older normal text window command. This one is obviously more powerful and has the benefit of being resolution independent. When working with [text variables](5.1-text-variables.md) to query the status or configuration of text windows, some text variables cannot query particular pieces of information about extended text windows (eg, `$TWX0$`, `$TWY0$`, `$TWX1$` and `$TWY1$`). The types of information that cannot be obtained are the text cell coordinates of the upper-left and lower-right corners of the extended text window - there aren't any - they're specified in graphical coordinates, not in text coordinates like with the RIP_TEXT_WINDOW command. The `$ISEXTWIN$` variable reports whether a given window is an extended one. See these text variables for more details about this kind of situation.
previous_implementation_evidence.reason: Connected established-window cell queries use the same loaded MAF metrics as extended fitting/rendering. Extended windows reject omitted-type cell-coordinate requests with -1; explicit graphical DEVICE/WORLD requests use stored unclipped geometry. Ambiguous far TEXT default forms are separately blocked by B108.

previous_implementation_evidence.text: If no parameters are specified, then this command returns the height of the current text window in text cells (lines). previous_implementation_evidence.text: If the domain parameter is omitted, then it automatically defaults to WORLD (except for the TEXT type, which defaults to the height of the text window in lines of text). previous_implementation_evidence.text: The BOUND parameter refers to the text window's bounding rectangle. It is the absolute exterior that the text window may extend to. previous_implementation_evidence.heading: $TWH$
previous_implementation_evidence.text: The CELL parameter indicates that you are inquiring about the height of a character cell used in the text window. The height of a cell is based on the font number and resolution currently in use on the actual destination RIPscrip software package. Under 640x350, this was typically 8x8 for font #0 (ie, in RIPscrip 1.54). This may be different now at varying resolutions. So, if you are running at a resolution of 640x350 and you inquire about a text window's cell height for a text window using font #0, then it most likely will return a result of 8 pixels (in device coordinates). The actual value in world coordinates could vary well be different based on the size of the world coordinate resolution frame. _(v2.A4)_

previous_implementation_evidence.heading: $TWH$
previous_implementation_evidence.text: The "TEXT" type indicates that you are requesting information about the text window sub-section of the text window definition. If the domain parameter is specified, then you are requesting the actual height of the text window display area in "lines of text". This can also be retrieved if the domain parameter is "ROWS". This particular domain parameter known as "ROWS" is only valid for a type parameter of "TEXT". Using it in any other context is considered a syntax error. If the domain parameter is specified, and it is set to "WORLD", then the pixel height of the display region is being requested in world coordinates. If domain is set to DEVICE, then you are requesting the height of the display region in actual hardware pixel coordinates. _(v2.A4)_

previous_implementation_evidence.heading: $TWW$
previous_implementation_evidence.text: The CELL parameter indicates that you are inquiring about the width of a character cell used in the text window. The width of a cell is based on the font number and resolution currently in use on the actual destination RIPscrip software package. Under 640x350, this was typically 8x8 for font #0 (ie, in RIPscrip 1.54). This may be different now at varying resolutions. So, if you are running at a resolution of 640x350 and you inquire about a text window's cell width for a text window using font #0, then it most likely will return a result of 8 pixels (in device coordinates). The actual value in world coordinates could vary well be different based on the size of the world coordinate resolution frame. _(v2.A4)_

previous_implementation_evidence.heading: $TWW$
previous_implementation_evidence.text: The "TEXT" type indicates that you are requesting information about the text window sub-section of the text window definition. If the domain parameter is specified, then you are requesting the actual width of the text window display area in "columns of text". This can also be retrieved if the domain parameter is "COLS". This particular domain parameter known as "COLS" is only valid for a type parameter of "TEXT". Using it in any other context is considered a syntax error. If the domain parameter is specified, and it is set to "WORLD", then the pixel width of the display region is being requested in world coordinates. If domain is set to DEVICE, then you are requesting the width of the display region in actual hardware pixel coordinates. _(v2.A4)_

previous_implementation_evidence.heading: $TWX0$
previous_implementation_evidence.text: If no type parameter is specified (as previously described), then the text window's upper-left X coordinate is returned in text coordinates. This is to maintain backward compability with older RIPscrip v1.54 related commands. In fact, this is not the best way of determining where the text window is on the screen - graphical coordinates are a much better method. If a text window is defined with the RIP*TEXT_WINDOW command where you specify the location of the text window solely on the basis of text coordinate X/Y data, then this form of this command will return a number indicating which X character cell the text window starts at. If the text window is defined using the RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW command, where the upper-left corner of the text window might not start on an even multiple of the window's cell size, then this command returns a value of "-1" to indicate that the desired request cannot be processed because the text window isn't the right kind of text window. In this manner, the value "-1" is used to indicate that an error has occurred with this command. *(v2.A4)\_

previous_implementation_evidence.heading: Face Extents and Input Eligibility

previous_implementation_evidence.text: Keep one logical outline metric snapshot per RIP interpreter/drawing context. It is shared across its ports and styles; it is neither a port cursor nor a STYLE-table member. A snapshot contains the realized face/size metric map `r[c]`, **X DPI `Dx` at preparation**, spacing `P` and flag `0x0400`, and realized horizontal span `B`. Atomic preparation preserves every old field on error; bounded unsigned-byte measurement uses stored X DPI, full finite length and checked wide sums before the final signed-WORD handoff. retired_source_units.text: For `[N:]` outside a grouped association, ordinary storage remains the existing plain slot operation. These baselines/publication tags clarify lifetime; they add no new wire syntax. A later explicit assignment is not lost merely because an old selected field is deleted. Mouse-field deletion removes its associations and reassembles affected publications but preserves ordinary baselines. For SOFT/drawing reset, preserve the already effective slot values as ordinary definitions before discarding deleted owners and their publication tags. retired_source_units.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
retired_source_units.text: Every pre-defined [text variable](../../glossary.md) known for RIPscrip 3.x, with its parameter form, type, effect, and evidence status, linked to its full entry. **Value** variables return text to the host; **Active** variables perform an action on the terminal (some also return data when used to query). Parameters shown in parentheses are optional unless the full entry says otherwise; the 2.0 parameterized forms supersede the 1.54 fixed names (`$SAVE(8)$` vs `$SAVE8$`). The 3.x inventory combines the original driver’s 179 registrations with the RIPtel help files (roughly 60 data-returning and 60 command-performing variables), the demo corpus (269 distinct `$…$` forms in shipping scripts), and SyncTERM's 103-entry built-in table.
retired_source_units.reason: Index wording about parameterized versus fixed aliases is tracked by editorial follow-up #138; detailed 5.1 entries explicitly retain all twenty numbered screen aliases. The broader inventory remains unreviewed.

retired_source_units.heading: $RCB$
retired_source_units.text: This Active Text Variable restores the Clipboard from a previously executed [`$SCB$`](#scb) command. Not only are the clipboard contents saved, but so is the last clipboard location, so Paste Clipboard ([`$PCB$`](#pcb)) restores the clipboard's contents AND location.
retired_source_units.reason: RCB now restores saved clipboard selection, PORT definitions and offscreen contents through real sessions. The remembered source/destination rectangles consumed by PCB are not implemented, so this combined contents/location claim remains pending.

retired_source_units.heading: $RCB$
retired_source_units.text: If you do not specify a slot parameter then the clipboard is restored from a slot-less file. It is not deleted so you can do multiple identical clipboard restorations. _(v2.A1)_
retired_source_units.reason: SCB/RCB execute in connected sessions against the existing PORT backup family. BASE is reusable; numbered/stack/protected lifetimes and generic COPY share the established manager. The snapshot owns clipboard selection by value alongside port/query/offscreen state; no onscreen pixels are saved. Remembered PCB source/destination rectangles remain separate pending work; no complete-PORT claim is inferred from these syntax/lifetime clauses.

retired_source_units.heading: $RCB$
retired_source_units.text: If you do specify a slot parameter then you may restore the clipboard from any of ten different clipboard slots (0-9). Once restored, the clipboard slot file is deleted. _(v2.A1)_

retired_source_units.heading: Success, Failure, Protection and Overlap
retired_source_units.text: Replacement/capture has its existing stage effects: if an old target was deleted, its old pair is gone; a surviving newly allocated clear target has **no pair** until an actual copy succeeds, even if an outer helper reports success after ignoring a blit/no-op result. A protected replacement rejection retains the old definition/pair. Allocation failure and current/clipboard changes keep the existing operation's documented or implementation-defined recovery scope; this metadata rule adds no rollback. retired_source_units.heading: Associated Template Ownership and Lifetime
retired_source_units.text: For `[N:]` outside a grouped association, ordinary storage remains the existing plain slot operation. These baselines/publication tags clarify lifetime; they add no new wire syntax. A later explicit assignment is not lost merely because an old selected field is deleted. For SOFT/drawing reset, preserve the already effective slot values as ordinary definitions before discarding deleted owners and their publication tags. This adopts the existing [SOFT template-preservation rule](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#state-that-survives), rather than importing the original field-clear helper's numbered-slot deletion. Do not evaluate any source while preserving those bytes. A reset explicitly clearing host-template storage instead clears the affected baselines/publications; table/style selection alone does not assemble or evaluate host text. Applying restored/replaced fields gives fresh instance tokens: any restored associated definition data belongs to those fresh owners, never to a suspended former instance. The [mouse-backup capture and publication rules](7.2-data-backup-areas.md#grouped-mouse-snapshots-and-template-publication) save persistent state/maps but exclude global baselines/publication tags, preserve current ordinary assignments, and rebuild only the surviving logical groups' current publications without host execution.

retired_source_units.heading: 5.4 Pop-Up Lists
retired_source_units.text: Pop-Up Pick Lists - host-defined selection lists that pop up on the terminal and splice the chosen entry's response into the [host command](5.0-host-commands.md) being built, legal anywhere a [text variable](5.1-text-variables.md) is. The mechanism carries into 3.x from 2.0 intact, with one 3.x extension: an optional pop-up position.

retired_source_units.heading: 5.4 Pop-Up Lists
retired_source_units.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP; SyncTERM (ripper.c:11356-11635, 11936-11948)._

retired_source_units.heading: 5.4 Pop-Up Lists
retired_source_units.text: _The 2.0 record is [5.4 of the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.4-popup-lists.md) (1.54 lineage in the [v1.54 page](../../1.54/ripscrip/5.4-popup-lists.md))._

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: Any place that you can use a text variable (Queries, Button and Mouse Field return strings, and Keystroke Macros), you can take advantage of a unique feature of RIPscrip - Pop-Up Pick Lists. A Pop-Up Pick List is simply a list that pops up allowing the user to choose from one of several available values. Whichever entry in the list is chosen will insert its associated response into the host command returned back to your host.

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: A list is created by putting the special list instructions inside two sets of parentheses, `((` and `))`. The list consists of an optional question followed by two colons (`::`), followed by one or more comma-separated list entries. For example, `((Send Email to?::Sysop,Cosysop,Joe))` says to pop up a list asking "Send Email to?", giving the choices of "Sysop", "Cosysop", and "Joe".
retired_source_units.reason: B159 requests exact list grammar, including absent and blank prompts, empty entries and malformed input.

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: The full 3.x syntax, with every extension in place:

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: | `((` … `))` | List delimiters |

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: | `*` | Response required - the user cannot ESC out of the list |

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: | `x,y:` | Pop-up position in [world coordinates](../../glossary.md); omit either value (keep the comma) to center on that axis _(new in 3.x - HLP)_ |
retired_source_units.reason: B159 requests the decimal position forms and independent omitted-axis mapping.

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: | `Question` | Prompt text; if omitted, the default is `Choose one of the following:` |
retired_source_units.reason: B159 requests the default and explicitly blank prompt outcomes.

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: | `::` | Separates the question from the entries |

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: | `response` | The text spliced into the host command when chosen |

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: | `@Description` | Optional display text shown in the list instead of the response |

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: | `~h~` or `_h_` | Hotkey markup around a character of the description; the first marked character is the active hotkey |

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: By default, if the user presses ESC instead of picking an entry in the list, then nothing is inserted into the text of the command. You can indicate that the user must pick an entry by putting an asterisk (`*`) at the beginning of the question - for example, `((*Send Mail to?::Sysop,Joe))` forces a choice of either Sysop or Joe.

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: In the previous examples, Sysop and Joe are the text responses that are inserted into your host command. They are also what is displayed in the listing. If you want to display something else in the listing instead of the return text, add an `@description` to the end of the entry. For example:

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text:
```text
((Send Mail To?::Sysop@Head Honcho,Cosysop,Joe))
```

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: ...would display a pop-up pick list of Head Honcho, Cosysop, and Joe.

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: One final feature allows you to specify a hotkey for each entry in the list. To highlight the first character of an entry (thus allowing that key to activate the entry), put a tilde (`~`) or an underline (`_`) before and after the keystroke: `_S_ysop` highlights the "S" in "Sysop". You can highlight more than one character, but only the first one will be the active hotkey. If you omit the second tilde or underline, then the remainder of the description will be highlighted.

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: > **NOTE:** If you use a tilde or an underline in the Text Response (not the description), those characters are inserted into your host command when it is transmitted to the host. You probably don't want to do this. Recommendation: only use hotkey features on list entries where you specify a description!

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: If you do not specify a question, then the list defaults to the question:

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists


retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text: Rules carried forward from 2.0, all confirmed by RIPtel's help: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
retired_source_units.text:
- Up to **64 entries** per list _(v2.A1)_; in earlier revisions of RIPscrip, a maximum of 20 entries was allowed. If the total number of entries makes the picklist too tall to fit on the screen, it must handle some form of scrolling mechanism. _(v2.A1)_
- In RIPterm version 1.52 and earlier, the total length of a pick list was 256 bytes; in version 1.53 and later, this limit was increased to 1024 bytes. _(v1.53)_
- The characters `!`, `\` and `|` have special significance in the RIPscrip language; to use them in a _Text Response_ they must be escaped with a backslash (`!` becomes `\!`, `\` becomes `\\`, and `\|` for the vertical bar). The hotkey markers `~` and `_` **cannot** be escaped - if they exist in a Text Response they are returned to the host, but everything after them is underlined and the first character is treated as the hotkey. Put hotkeys in descriptions, not responses.
- If the user presses ESC on a non-required list, nothing is inserted.
retired_source_units.reason: B159 requests verified bounds and the distinction between list-local delimiter quoting and ordinary pass unquoting.

retired_source_units.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists

retired_source_units.heading: Recursion into the HCL
retired_source_units.text: _Evidence: SyncTERM (ripper.c:11936-11948, 11890-11896)._

retired_source_units.heading: Recursion into the HCL
retired_source_units.text: The chosen response is not merely transmitted - it is **re-fed through the host-command interpreter**. A pick-list entry may therefore itself contain text variables, control characters, [playback directives](5.3-local-playback.md), or another pick list; SyncTERM implements exactly this (`do_popup`'s result recursing through `handle_command_str`), with recursion depth capped at 64. An entry prefixed `*` inside the option list forces that answer without user interaction - the mechanism SyncTERM uses to auto-answer forced choices. A menu that plays local scenes, a scene that pops another menu: pick lists plus `$>` playback form a small but genuinely programmable UI layer, years before such things were commonplace.
retired_source_units.reason: The RIPtel ordinary scanner splice conflicts with recursive execution and the option-star shortcut attributed to legacy SyncTERM.

retired_source_units.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 (mechanism; constructed example)._

retired_source_units.heading: Worked example: definition and response flow
retired_source_units.text: Consider a [mouse field](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md) whose host command embeds a pick list:

retired_source_units.heading: Worked example: definition and response flow
retired_source_units.text:
```text
!|1M0000122912340100000E((*Read which area?::MAIL@_M_ail,NEWS@_N_ews,FILES@_F_iles))^m
```

retired_source_units.heading: Worked example: definition and response flow
retired_source_units.text: The flow when the user clicks the field:

retired_source_units.heading: Worked example: definition and response flow
retired_source_units.text:
1. The terminal begins expanding the field's host command and encounters the `((…))` list definition.
2. A pop-up appears titled "Read which area?" listing **M**ail, **N**ews, **F**iles (hotkeys highlighted). The leading `*` means ESC is refused - the user must choose.
3. The user picks "News". The list expression is replaced by that entry's text response, `NEWS`.
4. Expansion continues - in 3.x, the response itself is re-fed through the interpreter (recursion above), so a response containing directives would execute them here. The trailing `^m` becomes a carriage return, and the terminal transmits `E NEWS` followed by CR to the host - which sees an ordinary command string and never knows a menu was involved.
retired_source_units.reason: The worked example depends on recursive execution. B159 requests the two-pass selection and transmission order.

retired_source_units.heading: Worked example: definition and response flow
retired_source_units.text: Nothing about the list persists after expansion; clicking the field again pops the list again.

retired_source_units.heading: Local Audio Playback - `$)FILE.WAV$`
retired_source_units.text:
- Audio plays **in the background, asynchronously** - graphics keep drawing and host data keeps arriving while sound plays.
- There is a **single playback channel**: starting a new file terminates whatever is currently playing.
- The reserved filename `$OFF$` (i.e. `1w` with filename `$OFF$`) silences the current sound.
- If the file does not exist locally, the directive does nothing; hosts deliver audio files ahead of time via block transfer ([6.2](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md)).
retired_source_units.reason: Session host commands share the waveform channel and resource loader. Native reply and pull fixtures cover ordered output, missing names, malformed media, and decoder availability.

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_SCROLL
retired_source_units.text: This command physically "copies" a rectangular region of the graphics screen up or down. The `<dest_line>` parameter is the Y position that is the destination scan line to receive the region. The Destination of the copy can overlap the original region, but cannot be on the same line. You cannot move the image area left or right at all. This command is designated for vertical scrolling of graphical data either up or down.
retired_source_units.reason: The RIPv3 source/destination geometry, clipping and fill rules require independent RIPtel 3.1 vectors. Prior adapter coverage asserted older RIP_COPY_REGION behavior.

In other words, you can scroll graphical data outside the current graphical viewport (even over the text window!). However, it does adhere to the boundaries of the current drawing port. _(v2.A3)_

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
retired_source_units.text: This command replaces the current port’s image rectangle and flags for subsequently displayed JPEGs, including local playback and received-image display. Coordinates use current world/device conversion; reversed corners are ordered. RIPtel 3.1 stores the converted far coordinates plus one. The setter accepts flags **0..63**, replaces the previous flags and rejects a larger value without changing the style. Unlike the [IMGSTYLE macro setter](5.1-text-variables.md#imgstyle), the wire handler can change a protected current port. _Evidence: original driver 0xc39a and [native style checks](../research/issue-21-image-style.md#native-style-checkpoint)._
retired_source_units.reason: Wire 1i is connected through the public void dispatcher. It decodes current ENV radix/XY width, orders corners, projects to DEVICE once and stores the extra far unit without viewport clipping. It accepts/replaces flags 0..63 and updates protected/inactive current ports. Four flags digits plus 0..12 reserved zeros and last-field shortening are supported; invalid flags/reserved data/coordinates retain state. Independent all-canvas matrices cover both radices, widths 2..5, all accepted flags, invalid 64, reversed coordinates, the exact full-reserved example, current selection and inactive/protection retention. IMGSTYLE shares projection but owns separate gates; JPEG wallpaper and delivery/whole-scene routing remain separate.

retired_source_units.heading: $IMGSTYLE$
retired_source_units.text: _Query or replace a drawing port’s JPEG image style_

retired_source_units.heading: $IMGSTYLE$
retired_source_units.text: The optional trailing keywords are case-insensitive, may repeat, and are OR’d together: **ASPECT=1, DELETE=2, NOCLEAR=4, USEPAL=8**. These replace the target’s flags. **Omitting all keywords sets flags to zero**, rather than retaining prior flags; there is no numeric-flags argument. Unknown keywords, a selector outside 0..35/CUR, nonnumeric coordinates or a set form with fewer than four coordinates cause a variable error without changing image state. Wallpaper bits 16/32 have no IMGSTYLE keyword in this driver. DELETE is stored but has no JPEG deletion effect; see the [flag table](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image_style).
retired_source_units.reason: The separate IMGSTYLE callback supports bare/current/named queries and decimal setters for screen/offscreen ports. Keywords are case-insensitive OR values, including duplicates; no keywords replaces flags with zero. Undefined/inactive targets return -1 without mutation/diagnostic; protected enabled targets query successfully and setters return no value without mutation/error. Valid setters temporarily select the target and restore the previous selection even on conversion failure. Queries convert the complete stored device boundaries through the live current WORLD, without subtracting the far increment. Independent literal replies, all keyword combinations, invalid parameters, state/selection recovery and every supported canvas are tested. Enclosing multi-action host expansion is a separate acceptance requirement.

retired_source_units.heading: Local Bitmap Playback - `$<FILE.BMP$`
retired_source_units.text: `$<FILENAME.BMP$` places a local bitmap (`.BMP`) file onto the screen through the current **image style** (`1i`, [RIP_IMAGE_STYLE](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image_style)): the bitmap is displayed inside the current image settings and adheres to them. This mode of displaying a BMP file is the only method for showing a BMP via the image-style settings. If no image style definition has been recorded, the bitmap is shown at the maximum size of the current viewport - scaled to fill it entirely.
retired_source_units.reason: The shared image style reference leaves bitmap-specific target geometry, edge handling, flags and automatic dithering undefined. The detailed portable placement contract covers JPEG.

retired_source_units.heading: Local Bitmap Playback - `$<FILE.BMP$`
retired_source_units.text: For the purposes of universality, the bitmap is shown using the current screen's color palette and "auto-dithering" mode. This directive is provided as a simple method of showing a bitmapped image from within a host command:
retired_source_units.reason: The shared image style reference leaves bitmap-specific target geometry, edge handling, flags and automatic dithering undefined. The detailed portable placement contract covers JPEG.

retired_source_units.heading: Local Bitmap Playback - `$<FILE.BMP$`
retired_source_units.text: Note that this uses the less-than sign, unlike the greater-than sign used for local RIPscrip playback - the opposite angle-bracket marks it as a low-level primitive playback, per the bracket mnemonic above.

retired_source_units.text: `$(FILENAME.JPG$` displays a compressed photographic image the same way - through the current image style, or full-viewport when none is recorded. The JPEG file is considered a higher-level object than a raw bitmap, so it uses the parenthesis prefix instead of the angle bracket. JPEG is the only supported photo format in the 3.0 driver:
retired_source_units.reason: Local HCL and wire IMAGE share the JPEG presenter. The connected fixtures cover active image style, computed and quoted filenames, current palette and retained source assets.

retired_source_units.heading: Local Scene Playback - `$>FILE.RIP$`
retired_source_units.text: The file replays as if it had arrived from the host - with one critical difference: **the data is echoed locally only, never sent to the host**. If the file is a RIPscrip scene, its graphics draw and any mouse fields it defines are created, which is how pop-up dialogs and entire menu systems run without host traffic. The file need not be RIPscrip at all - any text file, ANSI screen, or (in 3.x) flowed article text is legal; see the [Column Text System](3.1-column-text-system.md) for the non-RIPscrip case.

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
retired_source_units.text: This command instructs the remote terminal to playback a local `.RIP` file. The current execution of RIPscrip commands will be temporarily suspended and the contents of the designated RIP file will begin executing. Regardless of whether or not the current RIPscrip code coming across the modem is in the middle of a line or not, the RIP playback file will be assumed to start at the beginning of a line. Therefore, if a RIP_READ_SCENE command is located in a `.RIP` file, it must be the very last command on the line, followed by a carriage return instead of a command delimiter (`|`). This ensures that the loaded `.RIP` file will begin executing properly with the correct delimiters found in the correct places.
retired_source_units.reason: Connected 1R suspends its source, starts the file at a physical line beginning and resumes with the file's drawing and terminal state. Original nested delimiters and EOF dispatch await clarification.

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
retired_source_units.text: The RIP playback file can alter colors, fonts, or whatever. Once the playback of the file is complete, the remaining RIPscrip code that was temporarily suspended will resume execution. Any changes that appeared in the loaded playback file will remain in effect when the resumed code is processed - if you change a color or a font in the playback file and leave them changed, they remain in effect during the resumed execution.
retired_source_units.reason: Connected 1R suspends its source, starts the file at a physical line beginning and resumes with the file's drawing and terminal state.

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
retired_source_units.text:
- **Plain `.TXT` files**: `!|1R00000000DRAGON.TXT` inside an open `1e` column region flows the file's text into the columns, word-wrapped - it is _not_ parsed as RIPscrip. See [Flowing Whole Files](3.1-column-text-system.md#flowing-whole-files---1r-on-plain-text).
- **Overflow pages**: `!|1R00000000$OVERFLOW(1,CUR)$` re-reads the current page of a column stream's overflow buffer ([pagination](3.1-column-text-system.md#pagination---overflow-and-resetoverflow)).
- **Computed filenames**: `!|1R00000000<<IF $COLORS$<"256">>BLUEBACK.FN<<ELSE>>BLUEFADE.FN<<ENDIF>>` - the corpus's ubiquitous color-depth dispatch - and `$&MAIN_STORY$` variable dereferences (NEWSPAPR.RIP). See [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#inline-conditionals---if--elseif--else--endif).

retired_source_units.heading: State That Survives
retired_source_units.text:
- User/named variables and all template definitions survive; SOFT does not mean `$RESET(TV,...)$`, variable deletion or template deletion.
- All separately owned backup **base areas, numbered slots and stacks** survive for BUT, STYLE, PORT, TW, PAL, ENV, mouse fields and screen, with their stored state/pixels/protection. Live-table resets do not erase the independent backup objects. HARD reset and explicit backup-reset operations have different ownership.
- Offscreen/clipboard ports follow the live PORT protection rule: an unprotected clipboard is deleted and its assigned clipboard pointer cleared; a protected clipboard and assigned pointer survive. “Clipboard always cleared” and “all clipboard data always survives” are both incorrect. See [GET_IMAGE lifecycle](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_get_image).
- Global client ANSI/VT-102, communication/encoding preferences and the existing input-lock flag survive. Pending ANSI syntax is not copied into backup windows or canceled by this command.

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
retired_source_units.text: This command sets the rate at which [local RIP file playback](5.3-local-playback.md) is performed. By default, local RIP playback is done at full speed, which is dependent on your CPU, hard disk speed and many other factors. With this command, you can set the speed at which the playback is performed so that it approximates a particular baud rate. The setting remains in effect even after a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) command, so that a Reset command inside a local RIP file will not alter the playback speed in mid-stride. The setting remains in effect until changed explicitly by the user (if possible under the terminal software), or by the host via another RIP_BAUD_EMULATION command.
retired_source_units.reason: Local scene byte pacing uses the current ENV baud with an independent clock. Reset persistence awaits reconciliation with the recovered ENV reset contract.

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
retired_source_units.text: Typical settings for `<rate_val>` might be 300, 2400, 4800, 19200, etc. A value of 0 indicates that local playback should be performed at maximum speed (no baud rate emulation). _(v2.A3)_

retired_source_units.heading: Environment Table
retired_source_units.text: The environment data table is a central table for the maintenance of critical values that define the characteristics of the RIPscrip environment. This data table holds up to 36 separate environments. For RIPtel 3.1, world dimensions, Base Math, coordinate width, RGB precision and mouse pointer number belong to the environment. The inherited draft also describes baud-rate emulation in this table. **Current STYLE, BUT, PORT, TW and PAL selections are separate state:** the driver's environment selector does not save or restore those selections, their records, or mouse fields. The draft's proposed whole-context-swap example is not the shipped behavior. _Evidence: DLL; [activation derivation](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#ownership-and-switching-observations)._
retired_source_units.reason: CUR(ENV,n) and fixed-two-current-base-digit wire2E share protocol activation through the actual session-owned table. Unused targets take basic defaults; target mode fields overwrite the departing record before selection, bypassing protection but retaining its WORLD/pointer/baud. Existing native refresh reads the new current pointer. Other table selections/ANSI state/pixels/raster stay live. Numeric/CUR ENV entry COPY validates source and every destination before any mutation, carries source protection except to zero, defines targets, retains selection and permits repeated destinations. Native literal state/copy/split/failure tests and connected CP437/UTF8 expectations cover all presets/custom, protected/default/bypass cases, real plotted coordinates/pointer metadata, nonzero backups and zero-WORLD/error recovery. Header and other unfinished families remain separate; no ordinary text or RIP154 path changes.

SAVEALL/RESTOREALL dispatch TW, PORT, MOUSE, SCREEN, PAL, BUT, STYLE, ENV in exact order, continue after every failure without rollback and keep valid actions empty/nonfatal. Numbered restores retain all snapshots until a separate ordered delete phase, including failed unprotected snapshots; BASE stays reusable and POP consumes each successful family independently. Native event/ownership/failure tests and both TCP encodings cover executable behavior and independent expected colors, metadata and input. This accepts this syntax/lifetime/composition clause, not every subrequirement of each payload family; full PORT_COPY/PCB and remaining STYLE inventory stay separately pending.

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
retired_source_units.text: This command is intended to import some sort of text file document directly into a RIPscrip scene and format it nicely to fit inside a simple rectangular area. If the `<justify>` parameter is set to a value of "1" for a given RIP*REGION_TEXT line, then that line will be justified to both the left and right margins (the RIP_BEGIN_TEXT boundaries). This is so that the displayed text aligns on both sides with the invisible boundaries. This "justification" is done by splitting each RIP_REGION_TEXT line up into chunks of word-groups, broken up at their "white-space" locations. Each spacer is then padded by however many pixels are necessary to keep each spacer of approximately equal size. Only enough spare pixels are added to make sure that the right-edge of the text region aligns with the right border of the boundary. The result is a nicely formatted text block. *(v1.54)\_
retired_source_units.reason: The connected three-word and overwide cases verify signed padding with original MicroANSI glyph masks and a controlled device width.

retired_source_units.heading: Persistence
retired_source_units.text: Variables defined with the `+` directive (or [RIP_DEFINE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_define) flag `001`) are saved to a client-side persistent store and survive across sessions. Functionally this is nothing more than a **persistent key/value store** - variable name (≤ 20 characters) → string value (≤ 255 characters) - and that is all an implementation needs to provide. **How** it is stored is an implementation detail, not part of the protocol - RIPtel used a local database file, SyncTERM mirrors the behavior with `save_persistent_var`/`load_persistent_vars`, reloading persistent variables during interpreter startup; a new implementation may use any key/value-capable storage it likes so long as persistent variables survive across sessions and honor host deletion/protection semantics.
retired_source_units.reason: The key/value backend, owned snapshots/import and optional atomic client file adapter are implemented. Separate writer/reader processes verify disk persistence, including byte lengths, replacement and deletion; malformed loads preserve live tables. retired_source_units.heading: RIP_DEFINE
retired_source_units.text: This command is used to create a text variable on the Client (terminal) system. Simply put, a text variable is a piece of information assigned to an identifier that can either be saved to the terminal's [persistent variable store](../../glossary.md) (static variables) or kept in memory only (dynamic variables). Per the 2.00a4 draft, identifiers are 1-12 characters - any alphanumeric character and underscores (`_`), where neither an underscore nor a number can be the first character; RIPtel 3.1's help raises the name limit to 20 characters for the in-line variable syntax (see [5.0](5.0-host-commands.md#setting--reading-user-variables-from-host-commands)), while SyncTERM's reconstruction keeps 12. Values run to 255 characters; where and how persistent variables are stored is implementation-defined.

retired_source_units.text: The last flag determines whether the definition is interactive or not. An interactive definition will attempt to define the variable: if it already exists, the value pops up on the screen asking the user to confirm it is correct; if it does not exist, a similar pop-up box appears asking the user to enter data for the given variable. retired_implemented_claims.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
retired_implemented_claims.text: This command is intended to import some sort of text file document directly into a RIPscrip scene and format it nicely to fit inside a simple rectangular area. If the `<justify>` parameter is set to a value of "1" for a given RIP*REGION_TEXT line, then that line will be justified to both the left and right margins (the RIP_BEGIN_TEXT boundaries). This is so that the displayed text aligns on both sides with the invisible boundaries. This "justification" is done by splitting each RIP_REGION_TEXT line up into chunks of word-groups, broken up at their "white-space" locations. Each spacer is then padded by however many pixels are necessary to keep each spacer of approximately equal size. Only enough spare pixels are added to make sure that the right-edge of the text region aligns with the right border of the boundary. The result is a nicely formatted text block. *(v1.54)\_
retired_implemented_claims.reason: The connected three-word and overwide cases verify signed padding with original MicroANSI glyph masks and a controlled device width.

retired_implemented_claims.heading: RIP_END_TEXT
retired_implemented_claims.text: In 3.x it flushes pending text, closes the selected article’s overflow outputs and deactivates flow for both the [RIP_BEGIN_TEXT](#rip_begin_text)/[RIP_REGION_TEXT](#rip_region_text) form and the [`1e` column-region](3.1-column-text-system.md#defining-a-column-region---1e) form. It retains definitions, selection and paging state; it is not an overflow reset. The scene-end `#` also reaches this operation. _Evidence: DLL; [derivation](../research/issue-4-column-overflow.md)._

A variable such as `$&MAIN_STORY$` supplies the filename; `$OVERFLOW(1,CUR)$` supplies a saved-page filename. These expressions return filenames, not the text content itself. Keep layout definitions and story text separate to reuse a template with different copy.

retired_implemented_claims.text: The file feeds the local RIP and terminal interpreters. Its input bytes stay local, and commands reached in the file can send normal replies on the connection. retired_source_units.text: **Mode distinction:** PUT/LOAD image modes are the operation for that image command; global W is not applied afterward. Image mode 04 inverts source image bits, whereas drawing W04 inverts destination bits. For 8-bit S=0x3C, D=0xA5, these give 0xC3 and 0x5A. See the [operation equations](../../2.0/techspecs/2.3-drawing-composition.md#operations-and-operands).
retired_source_units.reason: Connected 1P mode 04 complements the source, including tagged RGB clipboard pixels. The bitmap file loaders and the full RGB operation contract still require separate acceptance.

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_PUT_IMAGE
retired_source_units.text: The position on the active drawing port that is to receive the image is specified by the (x,y) parameters. These define the upper left corner that will be the rectangle to receive the image data. If any part of the image would go off the edge of the viewport (or the screen) then it is truncated appropriately. _(v2.A3)_
retired_source_units.reason: A real clipboard capture supplies the unscaled copy. Absent and same-port selections are no-ops. Current destination geometry controls placement and clipping.

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_PUT_IMAGE
retired_source_units.text: The image that is retrieved from the clipboard port does so based on the port's viewport (the entire contents of the viewport are copied to the active drawing port). If the clipboard port is only used with the RIP*GET_IMAGE command, then the viewport will be the full size of the port. If however, some port related commands are used on this clipboard port, then it is possible to alter the viewport inside this port. This gives you the ability to paste sub-areas of the port's actual image onto the destination drawing port. *(v2.A3)\_
retired_source_units.reason: The stored clipboard viewport is the source rectangle even when deactivated. The wire handler tests activation only on its destination. Connected tests use a narrowed, inactive source.

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_PUT_IMAGE
retired_source_units.text: NOTE: The 1-byte `<res>` parameter is RESERVED FOR FUTURE USE and should be set to zero.
retired_source_units.reason: Senders use zero. RIPtel discards the received fourth operand. SyncTERM validates the optional digit in current Base Math and ignores its value.

retired_source_units.heading: RIP_PUT_IMAGE
retired_source_units.text: **Remembered-pair completion:** a successful nonempty PUT_IMAGE is a named port transfer and [publishes its final pair on the current destination](7.0-drawing-ports.md#producers-and-publication). It uses the source's current logical viewport and its normal anchor/clipping/mode, without requiring a remembered pair on that source. Its documented same-port/absent-pointer no-op leaves all pairs unchanged. Source pair metadata remains independent of the clipboard image data.
retired_source_units.reason: Destination-owned optional DEVICE pairs are published by successful logical copy/blit stages only, with original coupled/fit classification and physical mapping retained. Capture/duplicate/auto-stamp/PUT_IMAGE already reach these shared producers on connections; drawing, image renderers and button redraw use separate paths. PCB selects the assigned clipboard by default or explicit decimal/CUR, reverses offsets under COPY without changing global state, snapshots overlap, and keeps all failures below the void parser. Native independent geometry/failure/lifecycle vectors and actual CP437/UTF8 TCP captures cover runtime use. PORT snapshots deep-own pair values/absence alongside their previously accepted definition/query/bitmap/pointer fields.

retired_source_units.heading: Success, Failure, Protection and Overlap
retired_source_units.text: For an existing destination definition, a command-defined no-op, wholly **logically** clipped rectangle, invalid/inactive/undefined operand, rejected request or failed transfer leaves its previous pair unchanged. A logically nonempty successful copy publishes even when pixels remain identical or physical clipping/sample rejection writes nothing, as defined above. Snapshot source pixels before overlapping writes, including distinct screen ports sharing one backing surface; this reads the source before writing the destination without choosing a scaling filter. If preparing that snapshot fails, there is no transfer/pair publication. A later rendering failure does not imply pixel rollback.
